sections.section_title: The Women at the Empty Tomb
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to describe the women coming at early dawn on the first day of the week to complete the burial anointing, finding the stone rolled away and the body of the Lord Jesus absent -- two discoveries that create the gap between what they expected and what they encountered.

sections.section_title: The Two Men and the Command to Remember
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to present two angelic messengers who ask the theological question 'Why do you seek the living One among the dead?' and command the women to remember Jesus's Galilean predictions about the Son of Man's necessary suffering, crucifixion, and third-day resurrection -- a command not to receive new information but to recall what was already spoken.

The neutral reading finds this passage to describe the women's report to the eleven and the broader community, its dismissal as 'nonsense' (leros -- delirious talk), and Peter's verification visit to the tomb where he sees the linen wrappings without the body and goes home 'marveling' -- between dismissal and belief.

The neutral reading finds this passage to introduce two disciples traveling away from Jerusalem to Emmaus, with the risen Jesus joining their journey while their eyes are divinely prevented from recognizing him -- a purposeful concealment that will be removed only through the convergence of scripture interpretation and the breaking of bread.

sections.section_title: The Disciples' Account of What They Know
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to present the Emmaus disciples' understanding of Jesus as 'a prophet mighty in deed and word' who was delivered to death by the chief priests and rulers, with their extinguished hope ('we were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel') and their knowledge of the women's report, the empty tomb, and the angelic testimony -- all facts present but failing to produce belief without the interpretive framework.

The neutral reading finds this passage to present Jesus's rebuke of the Emmaus disciples for being 'slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken,' his declaration that the Christ's suffering and entrance into glory were necessary (dei), and his systematic interpretation of the entire scriptural witness -- beginning with Moses and all the prophets -- as a unified testimony about himself.

sections.section_title: Recognition at the Breaking of Bread
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to narrate the moment of recognition: when Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives the bread (replicating the pattern of the feeding of the five thousand and the last supper), the disciples' eyes are divinely opened, they recognize him, and he vanishes -- establishing the community meal as the locus of encounter with the risen Jesus and the pattern of word-then-meal as the means of recognition.

sections.section_title: Return to Jerusalem and Mutual Testimony
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to describe the Emmaus disciples' immediate return to Jerusalem where they find the gathered community already announcing 'The Lord has really risen and has appeared to Simon' -- confirming Peter's restoration through direct encounter with the risen Jesus, fulfilling the 'turning back' predicted in 22:32.

sections.section_title: Jesus Appears to the Gathered Community
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to establish the physical reality of the resurrection with deliberate thoroughness: Jesus greets the community with peace, addresses their assumption that he is a spirit by showing hands and feet bearing crucifixion marks, inviting physical touch, and eating broiled fish before them -- demonstrating continuity of identity and bodily reality.

sections.section_title: The Scriptures Opened and the Commission Given
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to present Jesus's declaration that everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled, his opening of the disciples' minds to understand the scriptures, and the commission: repentance for forgiveness of sins to be proclaimed in his name to all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

sections.section_title: Witnesses and the Promise of Power
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to designate the disciples as witnesses of the events and to promise the Holy Spirit ('the promise of My Father') as the necessary empowerment for their mission, with the instruction to remain in Jerusalem until clothed with 'power from on high' -- establishing that the commission and the promise are inseparable.

sections.section_title: The Departure and the Return to the Temple
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage to narrate Jesus's ascension from Bethany while performing the priestly blessing (completing what Zechariah could not in 1:22), the disciples' worship of the ascending Jesus, and their return to Jerusalem with great joy to praise God continually in the temple -- closing the Gospel's structural circle from temple to temple, from a mute priest to a worshiping community.
